newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs plan major debate on single currency.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs plan major debate on single currency.

text.p: Following the decision by European Union finance ministers on Sunday to readmit the Italian lira to the European Monetary System, Euro-MPs embark on Wednesday on a comprehensive debate on the euro.

If the terms of the Maastricht Treaty are strictly applied, Italy, like the other EU member states, will have to belong to the ERM for two years before it can participate in the single European currency.
But Dutch Soclialist Alman Metten is expected to recommend a more flexible interpretation of the rules.

Kicking off the European Parliament's debate, Metten will say that the treaty requires the member states to remain within the permitted margin for currency fluctuations for two years without devaluing against another European currency.
But, he will say, this does not oblige them formally to belong to the ERM.
Metten is keen for the largest possible number of member states to be able to take part in economic and monetary union (EMU).

His worries that too strict an interpretation of the treaty will cut most member states out of EMU are fuelled by recent reports from the European Monetary Institute (EMI) and the European Commission that a majority of EU countries currently do not meet the crucial economic convergence criteria.
Apart from exchange rate stability, member states will be judged on their record in controlling inflation, deficit and debt.
Metten will point out that ECOFIN ministers have a key role in judging what constitutes an "excessive", and therefore disqualifying, deficit and will urge them to be magnanimous in their decisions.

At the same time, parliament will examine two draft regulations -- COM(96)496 -- whose aim is to ensure that governments continue strictly to control their budgets once EMU is in place by means of an early warning system for excessive deficits and sanctions for those who step out of line.
Like Metten, Greek Christian Democrat Efthymious Christodoulou is concerned that the criteria for judging deficits should not be over-dogmatic.

Their concerns about excessive rigidity are not expected to influence parliament's decision to approve on Thursday a six- month extension of Alexander Lamfalussy's mandate as head of the EMI (until 30 June 1997).
Euro-MPs are also due to agree that Wim Duisenberg, the current head of the Dutch central bank, should take over as Lamfalussy's successor.
Lamfalussy said on Friday he thought there should be a 15 percent margin of fluctuation between the euro and other European currencies in the future version of the EMS.
According to German Christian Democrat Karsten Hoppenstedt, several other practical measures will be needed for the introduction of the single currency in 1999 to be a success.

Hoppenstedt will recommend on Wednesday replacing national currencies by the euro as soon as possible. Until the end of the transition period, in 2002, shoppers should be given the price of goods in both euros and national denominations, he will say.
The Commission and many Euro-MPs believe legal provisions are needed to reinforce these measures, especially where price labels and contracts in national currencies are concerned.

Belgian Christian Democrat Fernand Herman will be recommending approval of draft regulations -- COM(96)499 -- which will prevent parties to contracts agreed in national currencies from trying to rescind or renegotiate the deals once the euro is introduced.
The regulations will also oblige retailers to use double pricing between 1999 and 2003.
Before the debate ends, Euro-MPs will discuss the effects of monetary policies on the real economy.
For British Socialist Lyndon Harrison, monetary policy is not just about price stability, even though this is the main goal.
Harrison believes other indicators have to be taken into account too, including labour costs, unemployment rates, investment models and progress made towards completing the internal market.
